summary:
Seychelles repealed Penal Code Section 151 in 2016, ending a colonial-era offence that had carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex intimacy. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised under the current Penal Code.

The Constitution guarantees freedom from torture under Article 16 and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex under Article 27. The constitutional list does not name gender identity expressly.

Section 5 of the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) adds sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status to protected characteristics, creating an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences.

The revised law increases prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward a victim's sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability. The Human Dignity Trust describes Seychelles as the second African country, after South Africa, to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

Seychelles does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions. In June 2015 two men, one a British national and one a Seychellois national, were married at the British High Commission in Seychelles by the British High Commissioner; the ceremony took place through a foreign mission and did not create a marriage under Seychellois law.

For a trans visitor, the statutory position is one of decriminalisation and enhanced hate-crime protection on gender-identity grounds, with no local recognition of a relationship that would be read as same-sex under Seychellois law.
tangentialFactors: The Human Dignity Trust comparison places Seychelles after South Africa as the second African country to enact statutory protection against all forms of hate-based victimisation. That comparison concerns the scope of hate-crime law, not the recognition of relationships or gender identity in civil status.
localsOnly:
Seychellois nationals and residents have no access to same-sex marriage or civil unions under domestic law. The 2015 marriage at the British High Commission was solemnised through a foreign mission and did not establish a marriage recognised under Seychellois law.

The 2024 hate-crime amendments apply to residents as victims of violent offences motivated by hostility toward protected characteristics including gender identity and sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document police enforcement practice, entry or visa screening, document-marker rules, bathroom or facilities access, or access to gender-affirming care for trans travellers. One source states that legal and social conditions for visitors can vary from the statutory position but provides no specific incidents, enforcement data or locations.

No trans-specific violence data or hate-crime enforcement statistics are included in the inventory.
